**Reading Speed Limits**

Professional subtitling adheres to strict reading speed constraints to ensure viewers can comfortably read text while watching. The standard maximum is approximately 20 characters per second for most content, though this can vary by context—educational content may drop to 16-18 cps to allow comprehension of complex material, while action-heavy sequences might push toward 21-23 cps when visual density is lower. These limits are calibrated to average adult reading speeds and account for the cognitive load of simultaneously processing dialogue, visuals, and text.

**Line Length and the Two-Line Maximum**

Subtitle formatting follows the two-line maximum rule: text should never exceed two lines on screen. Each line typically caps at 42 characters for standard 16:9 aspect ratios, though this adjusts for different formats. This constraint forces subtitlers to prioritize clarity and concision, breaking dialogue naturally at clause boundaries rather than arbitrary points. The spatial limitation also ensures subtitles don't obstruct critical portions of the frame, particularly faces and action occurring in the lower third of the screen.

**Timing to Scene Cuts**

Precise timing synchronization with scene transitions is essential for professional subtitling. Subtitles should typically appear 1-2 frames before dialogue begins and disappear 1-2 frames after it ends, creating a buffer that prevents jarring on-screen appearance. When scenes cut, subtitles must terminate with the outgoing scene and new ones begin with the incoming one—overlapping cuts break the illusion. Skilled subtitlers use this timing flexibility to reinforce scene changes and maintain viewer immersion by treating subtitle rhythm as part of the overall editorial pacing.
